correctness.rationale: Global absolute-coordinate folding is 1-Lipschitz on every rectifiable boundary path and has a sign-reflection inverse for any prescribed endpoint; the folded two-simplex union is developed isometrically to a Euclidean pair of simplices; the segment between developed endpoints crosses the equatorial simplex at an explicit convex combination, so Euclidean lower bound and boundary upper bound agree. Coordinate algebra yields the 4t/(n-1) excess. Exact stretch follows from (1+t)^2 >= 4t, uniquely equal at antipode. Beta(1,n-1) simplex barycentric law yields the excess distribution and moment. The packaged checker passed 4002 exact-rational path cases, 23 mean-square cases and 180000 distribution trials; those tests support, not replace, the proof.

originality.rationale: Focused searches of research records, existing relevant claims, and primary studies did not reveal an explicit all-dimensional vertex-source cross-polytope metric identity or the complete squared-excess law. General polyhedral source-unfolding algorithms do not provide this closed formula as a stated implication without the family-specific folding argument. Saso–Schuerger–Shi cover the three-dimensional specialization: novelty attaches to n>=4 and the uniform-dimensional structure. This is a best-knowledge self-review, not a historical priority certification.
residual_risks: An unindexed all-dimensional closed formula, or an equivalently stated radial metric identity in an older source, could defeat priority.
General source-unfolding algorithms can in principle compute the distance on every fixed polytope; literature comparison distinguishes an explicit all-dimensional formula from generic computability.
The 2024 octahedral all-pairs formulas cover the n=3 specialization, which is excluded from novelty claims.

value.rationale: An exact universal pointwise intrinsic-to-extrinsic metric law on a canonical high-dimensional regular polytope is a natural geometric classification, not an arbitrary slice. The unique antipodal sharp dilation and full surface-area detour distribution follow with dimension-dependent exponents and reveal a sharp separation of worst versus typical squared excess (orders 1/n and 1/n^2). These formulae supply all-dimensional benchmarks for polyhedral geodesics; n=3 is acknowledged as previously covered.
